title: Sustainable Web Design, An Excerpt
summary: In the 1950s, many in the elite running community had begun to believe it wasn’t possible to run a mile in less than four minutes. Runners had been attempting it since the late 19th century and were beginning to draw the conclusion that the human body simply wasn’t built for the task. But on May 6, 1956, Roger Bannister took everyone by surprise. It was a cold, wet day in Oxford, England—conditions no one expected to lend themselves to record-setting—and yet Bannister did just that, running a mile in 3:59.4 and becoming the first person in the record books to run a mile in under four minutes. This shift in the benchmark had profound effects; the world now knew that the four-minute mile was possible. Bannister’s record lasted only forty-six days, when it was snatched away by Australian runner John Landy. Then a year later, three runners all beat the four-minute barrier together in the same race. Since then, over 1,400 runners have officially run a mile in under four minutes ; the current record is 3:43.13, held by Moroccan athlete Hicham El Guerrouj. We achieve far more when we believe that something is possible, and we will believe it’s possible only when we see someone else has already done it—and as with human running speed, so it is with what we believe are the hard limits for how a website needs to perform. summary: Antiracist economist Kim Crayton says that “intention without strategy is chaos.” We’ve discussed how our biases, assumptions, and inattention toward marginalized and vulnerable groups lead to dangerous and unethical tech—but what, specifically , do we need to do to fix it? The intention to make our tech safer is not enough; we need a strategy. This chapter will equip you with that plan of action. It covers how to integrate safety principles into your design work in order to create tech that’s safe, how to convince your stakeholders that this work is necessary, and how to respond to the critique that what we actually need is more diversity. (Spoiler: we do, but diversity alone is not the antidote to fixing unethical, unsafe tech.) It’s a methodology I created in 2018 to capture the various techniques I was using when designing products with safety in mind. Whether you are creating an entirely new product or adding to an existing feature, the Process can help you make your product safe and inclusive. summary: Do you find yourself designing screens with only a vague idea of how the things on the screen relate to the things elsewhere in the system? title: Designers, (Re)define Success First
summary: About two and a half years ago, I introduced the idea of daily ethical design . It was born out of my frustration with the many obstacles to achieving design that’s usable and equitable; protects people’s privacy, agency, and focus; benefits society; and restores nature. I argued that we need to overcome the inconveniences that prevent us from acting ethically and that we need to elevate design ethics to a more practical level by structurally integrating it into our daily work, processes, and tools. Unfortunately, we’re still very far from this ideal. At the time, I didn’t know yet how to structurally integrate ethics. Yes, I had found some tools that had worked for me in previous projects, such as using checklists, assumption tracking, and “dark reality” sessions, but I didn’t manage to apply those in every project. I was still struggling for time and support, and at best I had only partially achieved a higher (moral) quality of design—which is far from my definition of structurally integrated . I decided to dig deeper for the root causes in business that prevent us from practicing daily ethical design. Now, after much research and experimentation, I believe that I’ve found the key that will let us structurally integrate ethics. And it’s surprisingly simple! title: Mobile-First CSS: Is It Time for a Rethink?
summary: The mobile-first design methodology is great—it focuses on what really matters to the user, it’s well-practiced, and it’s been a common design pattern for years. So developing your CSS mobile-first should also be great, too…right? Well, not necessarily. Classic mobile-first CSS development is based on the principle of overwriting style declarations: you begin your CSS with default style declarations, and overwrite and/or add new styles as you add breakpoints with min-width media queries for larger viewports (for a good overview see “ What is Mobile First CSS and Why Does It Rock? ”). But all those exceptions create complexity and inefficiency, which in turn can lead to an increased testing effort and a code base that’s harder to maintain. Admit it—how many of us willingly want that? On your own projects, mobile-first CSS may yet be the best tool for the job, but first you need to evaluate just how appropriate it is in light of the visual design and user interactions you’re working on. title: The Wax and the Wane of the Web
summary: I offer a single bit of advice to friends and family when they become new parents: When you start to think that you’ve got everything figured out, everything will change. Just as you start to get the hang of feedings, diapers, and regular naps, it’s time for solid food, potty training, and overnight sleeping. When you figure those out, it’s time for preschool and rare naps. The cycle goes on and on. The same applies for those of us working in design and development these days. Having worked on the web for almost three decades at this point, I’ve seen the regular wax and wane of ideas, techniques, and technologies. Each time that we as developers and designers get into a regular rhythm, some new idea or technology comes along to shake things up and remake our world. How we got here I built my first website in the mid-’90s. Design and development on the web back then was a free-for-all, with few established norms. For any layout aside from a single column, we used table elements, often with empty cells containing a single pixel spacer GIF to add empty space. We styled text with numerous font tags, nesting the tags every time we wanted to vary the font style. And we had only three or four typefaces to choose from: Arial, Courier, or Times New Roman. title: User Research Is Storytelling
summary: Ever since I was a boy, I’ve been fascinated with movies. I loved the characters and the excitement—but most of all the stories. I wanted to be an actor. And I believed that I’d get to do the things that Indiana Jones did and go on exciting adventures. I even dreamed up ideas for movies that my friends and I could make and star in. But they never went any further. I did, however, end up working in user experience (UX). Now, I realize that there’s an element of theater to UX—I hadn’t really considered it before, but user research is storytelling. And to get the most out of user research, you need to tell a good story where you bring stakeholders—the product team and decision makers—along and get them interested in learning more. Think of your favorite movie. More than likely it follows a three-act structure that’s commonly seen in storytelling: the setup, the conflict, and the resolution. The first act shows what exists today, and it helps you get to know the characters and the challenges and problems that they face. Act two introduces the conflict, where the action is. Here, problems grow or get worse. And the third and final act is the resolution. This is where the issues are resolved and the characters learn and change. I believe that this structure is also a great way to think about user research, and I think that it can be especially helpful in explaining user research to others. summary: As a product builder over too many years to mention, I've lost count of the number of times I've seen promising ideas go from zero to hero in a few weeks, only to fizzle out within months. Financial products, which is the field I work in, are no exception. title: Design Dialects: Breaking the Rules, Not the System
summary: "Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L. Pike The web has accents. Tokens are phonemes, components are words, patterns are phrases, layouts are sentences. The conversations we build with users become the stories our products tell. But here’s what we've forgotten: the more fluently a language is spoken, the more accents it can support without losing meaning. title: Design for Amiability: Lessons from Vienna
summary: Today’s web is not always an amiable place. title: Designed for a Dead Language
summary: Every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin. Understanding why that happened is a more useful design lesson than anything the apps themselves will teach you. In 1788, Prussia introduced the Abitur, a standardized national examination required for entry into universities and the civil service. To pass it, students needed to demonstrate measurable, gradable knowledge. The system needed to teach language to large classrooms, produce consistent outcomes, and do it with one teacher and thirty students. The educators responsible for designing this system reached for the only teaching template they had, one that had been used in European schools for two centuries: the method developed to teach Latin. Latin, by 1788, was a dead language. Nobody needed to speak it. The scholars who studied it were reading Cicero and Virgil, not conducting conversations. The method built around it, memorizing grammar rules, constructing translations, analyzing written texts, reflected that reality exactly. Oral skills were irrelevant. title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. summary: Neuropixels のニュースから考える、分子構造ビューアの次のインターフェース Neuropixels の新型プローブのニュースを読んで、しばらく画面の前で固まってしまった。脳の何千ものニューロンの活動を、一本のシリコンシャンクに沿って同時に拾う。あの密度と帯域の話を眺めていると、自分がふだん向き合っている分子の座標データのことが、急に遠く感じられた。 私が去年の秋に始めたのは、ある酵素の小さなリガンド結合ポケットを、構造ビューアで一日中ぐりぐり回す作業だった。きっかけは地味だ。大学院の同期が「このポケット、論文の図だと平面的すぎて分からん」とぼやいていて、じゃあ自分で描き直してみるか、と思っただけ。ノートPC のファンが唸る音、深夜のコーヒーの苦味、何度も同じ残基をクリックしては「あ、違う」と戻す指の動き。あの数週間は、正直かなり孤独だった。 最初は市販のビューアをいくつか試した。でも、どれも座標を読むことはできても、私が知りたかった「この側鎖が本当にそこに収まっているのか」という感覚には届かなかった。ある夜、リガンドの回転を何十回もやり直しているうちに、ふと気づいた。私は構造を眺めているのではなく、構造に翻弄されていた。座標は静的で、私の操作だけが右往左往している。ニューロンの話でいう「同時に何千も」とは正反対の、貧しい対話だった。 転機は、PDB のエントリを丸ごと手元に持ってきて、ローカルで回し始めたことだった。ネットワークの往復をなくすだけで、操作のリズムが変わった。指の動きと画面の反応のあいだにあった、あの小さな苛立ちが消えていく。特定のポケットに残基を固定して、そこだけを何度も見返す。派手なことは何もしていない。でも、同じ場所を何度も訪れるうちに、私はそのポケットの「癖」のようなものを、少しずつ体で覚えていった。 そこから先は、自分のための小さな道具を足していった。構造データは RCSB PDB から落とし、残基の位置をスクリプトで一覧にして、目で追う場所を絞る。ビューアの上でリガンドを少しずつ動かし、ぶつかりそうな原子の距離だけを数字で確かめる。派手な可視化より、地味な照合のほうが、私には効いた。ある晩、これまで何度も「合わない」と切り捨てていた配置が、すっと収まる位置に落ち着いた。あのときの、静かな「あ」という声。誰も聞いていない部屋で、私はひとりで笑ってしまった。 ニューロンの話に戻ると、あのニュースが面白いのは、計測の密度が上がるほど、そのあとにある「解釈」の設計が問われるからだと思う。生データをそのまま並べても意味にはならない。どこを固定し、どこを動かし、何度も同じ場所に戻れるか。それは分子の構造を眺めるときと、たぶん同じ種類の仕事だ。ツールは、私の手を速くするためではなく、私の視線を深くするためにある。 だから私にとって、良いビューアとは機能の一覧ではない。同じポケットに何度も帰ってこられる、静かな場所のことだ。Neuropixels が脳の解像度を上げていくなら、こちらの解像度も、指と目のあいだの解像度を上げていきたい。あの夜みたいに、ふと手が止まって、でもまた動き出す。そんな作業の続きを、あなたもどこかで始めているのかもしれない。

title: Tabs in One: agrupa totes les pestanyes del Chrome en una sola columna (i allibera RAM)
summary: Si estàs llegint això, probablement tens més de 40 pestanyes obertes ara mateix. El Chrome menja 4 GB de RAM, el ventilador de l'ordinador portàtil crida i no trobes aquella pestanya que vas obrir fa 20 minuts. Vaig construir Tabs in One per solucionar exactament això. El problema La barra de pestanyes del Chrome és una franja horitzontal. Quan tens més d'unes 10 pestanyes, es redueixen a fils minúsculs. Perds la noció del que tens obert, els duplicats s'acumulen i el consum de RAM puja. Els gestors de pestanyes existeixen, però la majoria o bé: afegeixen encara una altra barra lateral que competeix amb el teu contingut, o bé requereixen compte / subscripció per a funcions bàsiques, o bé estan abandonats. Què fa Tabs in One Tabs in One recull totes les pestanyes obertes en una pàgina neta d'una sola columna . Quan l'actives, cada pestanya oberta es mou a aquesta pàgina i les pestanyes originals es tanquen — la RAM s'allibera immediatament. Pots restaurar qualsevol pestanya (o totes) com a pestanyes normals amb un sol clic, sense perdre res. Funcions principals: Vista d'una sola columna — cada pestanya com una fila llegible amb títol i URL, sense més favicons minúsculs. Restauració amb un clic — recupera les pestanyes individualment o totes alhora. Només enllaços únics — si la pàgina del gestor ja és oberta, només s'hi afegeixen els enllaços únics nous.
